name: Divide, XOR, and Conquer
description: You are given an array of $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$. In one operation you split the array into two parts: a non-empty prefix and a non-empty suffix. The value of each part is the bitwise XOR of all elements in it. Next, discard the part with the smaller value. If both parts have equal values, you can choose which one to discard. Replace the array with the remaining part. The operations are being performed until the length of the array becomes $$$1$$$. For each $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$), determine whether it is possible to achieve the state when only the $$$i$$$-th element (with respect to the original numbering) remains. Formally, you have two numbers $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$, initially $$$l = 1$$$ and $$$r = n$$$. The current state of the array is $$$[a_l, a_{l+1}, \ldots, a_r]$$$. As long as $$$l \lt r$$$, you apply the following operation: Choose an arbitrary $$$k$$$ from the set $$$\{l, l + 1, \ldots, r - 1\}$$$. Denote $$$x = a_l \oplus a_{l + 1} \oplus \ldots \oplus a_k$$$ and $$$y = a_{k + 1} \oplus a_{k + 2} \oplus \ldots \oplus a_{r}$$$, where $$$\oplus$$$ denotes the bitwise XOR operation. If $$$x \lt y$$$, set $$$l = k + 1$$$. If $$$x \gt y$$$, set $$$r = k$$$. If $$$x = y$$$, either set $$$l = k + 1$$$, or set $$$r = k$$$. For each $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$), determine whether it is possible to achieve $$$l = r = i$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10\,000$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10\,000$$$). The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \le a_i \lt 2^{60}$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10\,000$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output a single string of length $$$n$$$ where the $$$i$$$-th element is equal to 1 if it is possible to achieve $$$l = r = i$$$ and is equal to 0 otherwise.
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1863F — Divide, XOR, and Conquer [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
